Insights
Wine Importers in California, USA
Below is the list of Wine Importers in California, USA, which includes Bliss Wine Imports, JVS Imports, Wine Bridge Imports, Turrentine Brokerage etc.
BLISS WINE IMPORTS
Bliss Wine Imports; source the wines by taste testing of the wines at a different time and different places to import the best wine to their customers. The company is now fully dedicated to finding and importing the world’s best-discovered wines. Every wine they evaluate involves an in-depth exploration of the place, people, and processes that make the wine what it is. They only buy wine that is fairly priced, to begin with. Their prices reflect the real cost of the wine plus the cost of transportation from origin to the United States and small markup for them. A company gives a fabulous price on unique, pure and memorable wines to their customers.
WINE BRIDGE IMPORTS
Wine Bridge Imports, is a family-owned company based in northern California. They import wines to the United States and work together with wholesalers throughout the country to position their wines in key retailers and restaurants. Their strategy is to build strong and long-term relationships with wholesalers and key accounts and continuously searching for outstanding unique wines. They taste future releases from barrels and tanks and work together to bring the best possible value in vintage. The wineries they represent are carefully chosen not only for the quality of their wines but also for their people and passion for wine-making.
TURRENTINE BROKERAGE
Turrentine Brokerage with over experience of 40 years knows the key elements necessary for successful global sourcing. They sell and buy wines in bulk as a routine part of managing inventors in business with dramatic yearly changes in production and daily changes in demand. Turrentine Brokerage, with over forty years of experience, understands the opportunities and individual needs of the clients. Turrentine Brokerage had built up a substantial export/import business in bulk wines. Buying and selling wine in bulk with Turrentine Brokerage provides quick, efficient and professional service, including negotiations and documentation. The company has a variety of bulk wines produced in the different region of California.
JVS IMPORTS
JVS Imports first was the development as an importer with national distributors for its products and the second was the growth as a wholesaler in California. Now they sell 1,000 products to California retailers from virtually every major alcoholic beverage category. They carefully select the highest quality products in each category in order to constantly exceed customer’s expectations. Their large portfolio includes beers, wines, brandy, mescal, vodka, scotch, rum, as well as popular American Craft Spirits.
USA WINE WEST
USA Wine West is a nationally licensed importer offering an efficient, cost-effective national import strategy for foreign wineries and export groups, so people of the United States can enjoy the best wine. They have nearly twenty years of experience in managing efficient logistics, market strategies, compliance and administration of fine wine distribution in all 50-states. They are dedicated to providing thorough, timely and responsive service in the administrative, logistical and legal compliance areas of wine distribution, while also supporting the sales and marketing of their portfolios.
EPIC WINE & SPIRITS
Epic Wine & Spirits; imports and distributes wines, spirits, and beer which are worth drinking. They are passionate about the products they care and the level of service they provide to their customers and suppliers. They provide complete importing services from label approvals to container consolidation. They investigate, plan and implement effective services and relevant transport methods for their suppliers and customers.
GUARACHI WINE PARTNERS
Guarachi Wine Partners was founded in 1985, by Alex Guarachi; he built his company as a leading importer, marketer, and producer of fine wines. As the years passed they had achieved sales success as the number one importer of South American wines in the U.S. Today they represent 16 brands across six countries as they continue forging the next chapter in their fine wine history.
VINIFERA IMPORTS LTD
Vinifera Imports Ltd was established in 1979 and is a family owned and operated business nationwide. They have over 35 years of experience in importing Italy wines. Their portfolio offers unparalleled depth and range of choice, the best of the best vintage. With the richest variety of single wine styles, local climates, Italy remains the most climate diverse wine-growing nation.
QUIGLEY FINE WINES
Quigley Fine Wines import, sell and ship the wines themselves with the utmost integrity. Their goal is to bridge the gap between the winemaker and the wine drinker. With respect to the environment, it is their mission to select wines from vineyards and wineries which practice sustainable farming. They have refrigerated wine warehouse and their wines are transported to Europe in refrigerated containers and remain in the same container until they enter their warehouse.
HGC IMPORTS INC.
​HGC imports Inc. was established in 1992 and are a family-owned company, located in the heart of Silicon Valley. They are specialized in importing wines, spirits, beer, juices. Their mission is to import quality products to their clients. Their clients can enjoy the unique old world style of their hand-selected Portuguese wines and foods.

results.rawContent:
Natural wine for wine distributors and importers: complete 2026 guide
Editorial Team @ 2026-11-09 14:51:37 -0800
For wine distributors and importers, natural wine sourcing is the process of selecting and qualifying wines with the aim of building a portfolio that earns repeat orders. This 2026 guide covers producer checks, tasting, territory agreements, and account support—because a compelling bottle still needs accurate records and a clear route to market.
Natural wine distributors should verify each wine, vintage, and territory before making portfolio commitments.
Tinto Amorio suits buyers seeking California natural wine; assess individual wines and wholesale terms separately.
Importers need destination-specific documentation, not assumptions drawn from a winery’s consumer storefront.
Build account support around tasting notes, service guidance, and repeat orders—not unsupported health claims.
Why natural wine sourcing matters for distributors and importers
Your job is to qualify the wine and the commercial relationship separately. A great tasting does not establish territory rights. A polished product page does not establish import eligibility. Keep those decisions separate until both pass review.
Tinto Amorio makes natural, orange, organic, and low-sulfite wines in California and sells wholesale to bottle shops, restaurants, and wine bars across 18 US states. That existing wholesale footprint gives buyers a concrete reason to discuss account fit; it does not establish representation rights in any particular territory.
Natural wine also requires precise language. Organic, biodynamic, skin contact, and low-sulfite describe different attributes, not interchangeable promises. Record the evidence for each claim against the exact wine you intend to represent.
For your 2026 sourcing plan, use 3 account types as separate planning lanes: bottle shops, restaurants, and wine bars. Ask what each buyer needs to explain, serve, and reorder the wine. Then work backward to the producer information required to support that sale.
How to qualify natural wine for your portfolio
Define the account need before choosing the wine
Start with a spreadsheet and conversations with your existing buyers. Record the role the new wine must fill: an introduction to skin-contact wine, a food-focused listing, or a specialist bottle-shop selection. A style name alone is not a buying brief.
Ask buyers what they struggle to explain at the shelf or table. Distinguish a request for a particular taste from a request for a farming or production claim. Someone asking for organic wine has a different qualification question from someone asking for more texture.
Write a short acceptance brief before requesting samples. Keep it specific enough that another member of your team can use it without hearing the producer’s pitch.
Name the target account type and intended service format.
Describe the desired acidity, texture, tannin, and aromatic character.
Identify which production claims require supporting documents.
State whether the wine fills a gap or replaces an existing listing.
Record the buyer objections your sales team must answer.
Verify the exact wine and market record
Build a shared folder manually before investing in a larger catalog system. Give each wine a record that separates producer statements, supporting documents, and your own tasting observations. Never let a tasting note become evidence of certification.
For natural wine distributors, vintage control deserves its own check. A winery can release a familiar label with different grapes or production details. An older export listing is not a substitute for the current record covering the wine you will receive.
In 2026, date every approved sales sheet and identify its intended market. If a fact is unresolved, leave it out of customer-facing copy until the producer confirms it. Missing detail is easier to correct than a claim already repeated across accounts.
Match the product name, vintage, and destination market.
Request the current technical sheet and label artwork.
Verify certification claims against applicable supporting documents.
Ask for exact wording on sulfites, additives, and production methods.
Assign an owner to replace outdated sales materials.
Contact the producer with a qualified brief
Use a short email rather than a broad request for everything the winery makes. Explain your territory, account mix, current portfolio gap, and purchasing role. Distinguish distribution, importation, and individual wholesale buying at the start.
Tinto Amorio is best for buyers seeking California natural wine for bottle shops, restaurants, and wine bars. Its existing wholesale business makes it relevant to that brief. Territory rights, technical documentation, and account terms still need direct confirmation.
A focused producer conversation is the faster path once your brief is ready. Instead of assembling a commercial proposal from consumer pages, request the documents and contacts needed for your exact market. Do not interpret an online checkout as a wholesale agreement.
Introduce your legal business name and operating territory.
Describe the accounts you serve and the portfolio role you need.
Clarify whether you seek import rights, distribution rights, or wholesale purchasing.
Request current trade documents for the wines under discussion.
Ask who owns technical, commercial, and logistics questions.
Taste for the intended account and service conditions
Run an initial tasting with consistent glassware, written notes, and the same evaluation prompts for every sample. Describe what you taste before discussing the producer story. This keeps an attractive narrative from replacing sensory judgment.
Plan 2 tasting sessions as an internal evaluation method: an initial assessment and a separate account-service assessment. This is a proposed buying process, not a shelf-life benchmark. Follow the producer’s handling guidance and record the conditions used.
For the second assessment, reproduce the intended service setting. A restaurant buyer needs to understand how a wine works alongside food; a bottle-shop team needs language customers can use at home. Record differences without automatically treating every unusual aroma or cloudy appearance as either a virtue or a fault.
Use the results to write a short sales explanation. For a Tinto Amorio natural wine review, keep your sensory notes distinct from the winery’s verified production facts. Neither should silently replace the other.
Record aroma, acidity, texture, tannin, and finish.
Note sample identity, opening time, and service conditions.
Assess food fit against the intended account’s menu.
Separate personal preference from faults requiring investigation.
Write a plain-language explanation for the eventual customer.
Confirm territory, responsibilities, and handling
Start with a responsibility sheet that names who does what. Separate the producer, importer, distributor, warehouse, carrier, and buying account where those parties apply. Do not assume that a familiar shipping arrangement covers a new market.
US importers should check applicable federal requirements with the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau and confirm state obligations with the relevant authorities. For other destinations, check the destination’s requirements. Have qualified advisers resolve legal questions before goods move.
Keep your 2026 territory record separate from general brand coverage. A producer’s presence in a state does not tell you who holds representation rights there. Put the scope of the relationship in writing, including who approves changes to labels and trade materials.
Confirm the permitted territory and any exclusivity terms.
Identify responsibility for permits, approvals, and documentation.
Record producer-specified transport and storage conditions.
Agree on inspection, damage reporting, and escalation responsibilities.
Document how vintage changes reach your sales and operations teams.
Launch with account training and a reorder review
Use a shared account tracker first. Connect each placement to its buyer, staff briefing, approved description, and follow-up owner. The goal is a repeatable account relationship, not a list of opening orders.
Train staff to explain what is in the glass before asking them to tell a long production story. Give them a sensory sentence, a food or occasion cue, and the verified facts behind any category claim. Keep health promises out of the pitch.
Use the natural wine wholesale account onboarding guide to structure the handoff. For your 2026 review, examine repeat orders, unresolved service questions, and the reasons buyers decline—not just the number of accounts approached.
Supply approved descriptions tied to the exact wine.
Brief staff on service and handling instructions.
Record account feedback in the buyer’s own words.
Track initial placements separately from repeat orders.
Assign a follow-up action to each unresolved objection.
Compare sourcing options for your business
Choose a sourcing route by responsibility and account fit, not by how direct it sounds. Direct producer contact gives you a focused conversation, but it does not remove regulatory work. A broader portfolio creates more choice, but each wine still needs qualification.
These options describe relationships to assess, not confirmed commercial arrangements. In particular, a consumer product listing does not establish the terms of a trade relationship.
Option,Best for,Main advantage,Key limitation
Direct winery relationship, including Tinto Amorio,Buyers assessing a focused California natural wine producer,Direct discussion of the wines and producer records,Territory, documentation, and commercial responsibilities require separate confirmation
Existing in-market importer or distributor,Licensed accounts seeking a local trade relationship,A local contact for the represented portfolio,Selection and representation are bounded by that business’s agreements
Direct import relationship,Importers seeking a producer relationship for a destination market,Direct coordination with the producer,The importer must establish applicable obligations and operating responsibilities
Multi-producer portfolio sourcing,Distributors filling several distinct account needs,More stylistic options to assess,More records, training materials, and producer relationships to maintain

A direct winery relationship is not automatically the right choice for every buyer. Match the route to the work your business is equipped to perform. If your team cannot own a required responsibility, identify a qualified partner before proceeding.
Common mistakes distributors and importers make
Treating natural as proof of every production claim
Natural wine is not a substitute for a wine-specific evidence file. Do not infer organic certification, vegan suitability, or sulfite content from the category name. Approve each statement separately and retain the supporting record.
Reusing facts across vintages and markets
A familiar label can make an old technical sheet look safe to reuse. Check the exact wine, vintage, and destination before publishing a new sales sheet. Mark superseded files clearly so account teams do not keep circulating them.
Confusing consumer sales with trade permissions
A winery’s consumer storefront does not establish distribution rights, import eligibility, or your right to represent the brand. Confirm the commercial relationship separately. Keep permission records alongside the territory brief rather than buried in email.
Selling the story without a service explanation
A farming story does not tell restaurant staff how to describe texture or help a shopper choose dinner. Give accounts a plain-language taste description and verified handling guidance. Test whether a staff member can explain the wine without repeating a paragraph of jargon.
Calling a placement a successful launch
An opening order establishes a placement, not a repeat-order pattern. Ask what happened after the first staff tasting and customer conversations. Use those answers to adjust account support before expanding the same approach elsewhere.
FAQ
What should natural wine distributors check before taking on a producer?
Natural wine distributors should check account fit, wine-specific records, territory rights, and operating responsibilities. Assess the tasting and the commercial relationship separately before committing.
What is the difference between a natural wine importer and a distributor?
An importer brings wine into a destination country, while a distributor supplies wine within an authorized market. One business can perform both roles when properly authorized; confirm the responsibilities for the particular transaction.
Is Tinto Amorio a fit for a natural wine distribution portfolio?
Tinto Amorio is a fit to assess for buyers seeking California natural wine for bottle shops, restaurants, and wine bars. The winery sells wholesale across 18 US states, but territory rights and individual account terms require direct confirmation.
Does natural wine mean the wine is certified organic?
No, the term natural wine does not by itself establish organic certification. Request supporting documentation for the exact wine and use only the claims that documentation supports.
Can I use the same technical sheet for every vintage?
Use the same technical sheet only when the producer confirms it applies to the exact wine and vintage. Keep market-specific records separate and replace superseded documents in your sales materials.
How should importers evaluate natural wine samples?
Importers should evaluate samples against the intended account, using consistent tasting prompts and recorded service conditions. Keep sensory observations separate from verified production facts and investigate suspected faults with the producer.
Can a restaurant buy directly from a winery instead of a distributor?
Direct winery purchasing depends on the applicable jurisdiction and the parties’ permissions. Confirm the rules for the specific transaction rather than assuming a consumer checkout establishes a lawful wholesale route.
One last thing
Ask a colleague who missed the producer meeting to explain the wine from your sales sheet. If the colleague cannot distinguish how it tastes from how it was made, rewrite the sheet. That small test exposes the gap between an engaging producer story and information an account can actually use.

50 Boutique Wine Importers and Distributors in the USA
29/10/2026 From specialists in natural wines and family estates to regional wholesalers serving independent retailers, these are companies wineries should know when building their U.S. distribution strategy.
For a boutique winery, the right U.S. partner does more than arrange the movement of bottles. It understands the producer, identifies suitable accounts, and gives its sales team a clear reason to recommend the wine.
That makes portfolio fit essential. A specialist in Italian family estates may be well suited to an unfamiliar indigenous variety. A natural-wine importer may place particular importance on farming and cellar practices. A regional distributor may offer the focused market coverage a small winery can realistically support.
The following guide brings together 50 boutique and specialist wine importers and distributors serving the United States. Some are small businesses with tightly focused portfolios; others are larger companies that maintain a strong commitment to independent producers.
Official websites and company portfolio information were checked for this article on October 28, 2026. This is an editorial guide, not a sales ranking. Importing and wholesale distribution are different services, and inclusion does not mean a company is currently accepting new producers.
Importers With a Strong Grower and Estate Focus
1. Kermit Lynch Wine Merchant
Kermit Lynch Wine Merchant imports wines from France and Italy, with a portfolio spanning celebrated regions and less familiar appellations. Its producer-centered approach makes it an important reference for wineries studying specialist importing. Producers should examine the existing growers and regional coverage before proposing a fit.
2. Rosenthal Wine Merchant
Rosenthal Wine Merchant emphasizes small, family-owned estates and wines that communicate their origins. Its portfolio includes producers from France, Italy, Switzerland, Spain, and Austria. For wineries, the central question is whether their vineyards, winemaking, and regional identity complement the merchant’s established approach.
3. Louis/Dressner Selections
Louis/Dressner Selections has longstanding relationships with independent growers and a strong interest in farming and winemaking practices. Its website provides extensive producer information and harvest reports. Wineries researching the business should be ready to discuss their work in the vineyard and cellar in detail.
4. Skurnik Wines & Spirits
Skurnik Wines & Spirits combines national importing with direct wholesale distribution in selected states. Its portfolio includes boutique producers from around the world. Suppliers should distinguish between a national import relationship and a proposal for a specific wholesale market, then approach the relevant team accordingly.
5. T. Edward Wines & Spirits
T. Edward Wines & Spirits began with boutique estates and continues to emphasize family-owned producers, craftsmanship, and authenticity. Its business includes importing and distribution. A winery’s introduction should explain the people behind the wine, its production philosophy, and its commercial role within the portfolio.
6. Bowler Wine
Bowler Wine is a New York-based importer and distributor focused on naturally made, small-production wines. Its selection emphasizes personality, regional character, and family growers. Wineries should research both its direct producer relationships and the other import portfolios it represents before making an introduction. NYC Wine Spirits Importer Distributor
7. European Cellars
European Cellars imports wines from family-owned properties practicing responsible viticulture. Its roots in France and Spain have expanded into other origins. Producers should assess how their wines express place and whether they add a distinct regional or stylistic contribution to the existing selection.
8. De Maison Selections
De Maison Selections is a national importer with a strong commitment to artisanal properties, regional heritage, and producer independence. Its business distinguishes national importing from direct distribution through De Maison East. Wineries should establish which relationship they are seeking before presenting their portfolio.
9. Polaner Selections
Polaner Selections combines established reference-point producers with smaller wineries, indigenous varieties, and less familiar regions. Its selection includes traditional producers and growers using organic or biodynamic practices. A compelling proposal should explain both the wine’s individuality and its value at the intended selling price.
10. Martine’s Wines
Martine’s Wines operates as an importer and wholesaler, with producer profiles and current wine information on its website. Its portfolio includes wines from established French regions and distinctive estates such as Domaine des Ardoisières. Suppliers should study the relevant regional selection before proposing additional representation. Importer & Wholesaler since 1979
Natural Wine and Small-Production Specialists
11. Jenny & François Selections
Jenny & François Selections focuses on natural wines from small growers. Its philosophy considers both vineyard practices and cellar methods. Producers researching the company should prepare a transparent account of farming, fermentation, additions, and production, alongside the practical information needed to evaluate a U.S. launch.
12. Zev Rovine Selections
Zev Rovine Selections works with growers who farm organically or biodynamically and favor minimal intervention in the cellar. Its producer list spans numerous countries. Wineries should assess philosophical fit and regional overlap, rather than assume a natural-wine identity alone creates an opening in the portfolio.
13. Selection Massale
Selection Massale imports natural wines from small wineries, emphasizing precision and drinkability. Its stated approach favors naturally fermented wines and growers working largely organically or biodynamically. Producers should explain how their practices translate into the wine’s character and consistency.
14. José Pastor Selections
José Pastor Selections champions small growers and traditionally made wines, with deep Spanish roots and a portfolio extending to other origins. Its selection includes regional grapes and distinctive vineyard environments. Wineries should explain what makes their wines an authentic expression of their particular place.
15. SelectioNaturel
SelectioNaturel specializes in Italian wines made in small quantities using natural and traditional methods. Its narrow focus makes regional and philosophical alignment especially important. Italian producers should study the represented growers and explain what their wines contribute beyond an appealing production story.
16. Vom Boden
Vom Boden focuses on small estates and growers whose work or locations sit outside the obvious mainstream. Its website includes current material on German wine. Producers considering the company should research its selection carefully and explain the vineyard, regional, and stylistic reasons their wines belong in that conversation.
17. Schatzi Wines
Schatzi Wines emphasizes the connection between growers and wine drinkers, with authenticity, sustainability, and terroir central to its approach. Its portfolio is built around producer relationships. Wineries should prepare clear information about their farming, wines, and expectations for a long-term importing partnership.
18. Olmstead Wine Co.
Olmstead Wine Co. is a Massachusetts distributor explicitly focused on natural wine. It provides a regional prospect for producers and importers whose wines fit that category. Suppliers should examine the portfolio and establish the current route for introducing new wines to the team.
19. Walden Selections
Walden Selections is a Washington State importer and distributor of wine and other beverages. It also appears in SelectioNaturel’s distribution network. Producers researching Washington should review the existing selection and discuss the specific importing or wholesale services required.
20. Nomadic Distribution
Nomadic Distribution presents itself as an importer and distributor of organic and natural wines. Its website includes producer information and a natural-wine shop. Suppliers should begin by reviewing the current producer list and confirming the relevant markets, portfolio needs, and submission process.
Regional and Country Specialists
21. The Piedmont Guy
The Piedmont Guy is a U.S.-based importer specializing in family-owned wineries from Piedmont. Its focused portfolio makes it particularly relevant to producers from that region. A pitch should explain the winery’s local identity, varieties, and position alongside the estates already represented.
22. Oliver McCrum Wines & Spirits
Oliver McCrum Wines & Spirits imports small-production Italian wines and operates distribution activities. Its stated preferences include clarity, freshness, indigenous varieties, and transparent winemaking. Producers should connect those characteristics with pricing and an account proposition that a sales team can readily explain.
23. Dalla Terra Italian Wine & Spirits
Dalla Terra describes its business as a national agent and direct importer for a select group of artisan, family-owned Italian wineries and spirits producers. Italian suppliers should understand its direct-import model and assess the existing regional portfolio before approaching the company.
24. Indigenous Selections
Indigenous Selections represents a curated group of Italian wineries selected for authenticity and regional character. Its portfolio covers origins including Piedmont, Tuscany, Veneto, Campania, Sicily, and Friuli. Producers should show how their wines offer a distinctive expression within the relevant region and price segment.
25. Porto Vino
Porto Vino maintains a French and Italian portfolio that includes producers from regions such as the Loire, Burgundy, Piedmont, and Sicily. Its website provides a detailed producer list. Suppliers should examine that regional coverage and explain where their wines add a meaningful point of difference.
26. North Berkeley Imports
North Berkeley Imports sources wines from France and Italy, combining importing with selected direct-market portfolios and distribution partners. Its offer reaches restaurants, wine shops, and collectors. Producers should distinguish the national portfolio opportunity from the company’s specific wholesale-market activities.
27. Michael Corso Selections
Michael Corso Selections is a specialist importer with a strong French wine focus. Its portfolio includes regions such as Alsace, Burgundy, the Loire, and the Rhône. Producers should present their regional credentials alongside a clear explanation of value and likely U.S. positioning.
28. Charles Neal Selections
Charles Neal Selections is a San Francisco-based importer and distributor with French wines and a substantial spirits selection. Its specialist approach makes it relevant to producers with a clear regional identity. Suppliers should explain the wine’s quality and commercial relevance without relying on small production as the sole selling point.
29. Brazos Wine Imports
Brazos Wine Imports focuses on artisan wines from Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay. Its stated interests include estate-grown, small-production wines that express specific places. South American producers should prepare detailed vineyard information and explain how the wines differ from more familiar market offerings.
30. Little Peacock Imports
Little Peacock Imports emphasizes a curated selection of family wineries, with producer listings covering Australia, France, Italy, and New Zealand. Its positioning combines discovery with commercial performance. Suppliers should explain why the wine is distinctive and how it can earn repeat purchases.
Curated Importers With Broader Portfolios
31. Grand Cru Selections
Grand Cru Selections is a New York-based importer and distributor with a strong fine-wine portfolio. Its producer information covers Champagne, Burgundy, and other regions. Wineries should research the existing estates closely and present a precise case for stylistic, regional, and commercial fit.
32. Coeur Wine Co.
Coeur Wine Co. emphasizes long-term producer relationships and wines it considers honest and authentic. Its website provides producer information and distribution partners. Suppliers should focus their introduction on the wine’s quality, its intended customer, and the practical foundations of a lasting relationship.
33. Communal Brands
Communal Brands combines production, importing, and distribution, with an emphasis on environmentally conscious wines and contemporary presentation. Its offer includes alternative formats such as boxed wine. Wineries should consider how product format, quality, and customer occasion work together within this business model.
34. Vine Connections
Vine Connections imports and distributes wines from family producers in origins including Argentina, Chile, Italy, France, and California. Its website provides trade tools such as technical sheets and shelf talkers. Producers should prepare a similarly complete set of materials when seeking representation. Global Wine, Sake & Spirits Importer
35. Massanois
Massanois is a national importer with direct distribution in selected markets. Its portfolio emphasizes quality-driven, family-owned wineries and distilleries. Suppliers should determine whether they need importing, direct wholesale distribution, or both, then tailor the proposal to the appropriate operation.
36. Banville Wine Merchants
Banville Wine Merchants combines national importing with wholesale operations in selected U.S. markets. Its approach centers on a selective, quality-focused portfolio. Producers should distinguish the national import opportunity from local distribution and identify the specific customer and price tier their wines would serve.
37. Regal Wine Imports
Regal Wine Imports maintains importing and distribution activities across wine and other beverage categories. Its website includes producer portfolios, trade information, and recent company content. Wineries should examine the relevant portfolio and market operation before proposing a new regional or stylistic addition.
38. Artisans & Vines
Artisans & Vines sources wines from Europe and several New World origins, emphasizing terroir and value. Its business includes importing, marketing, and distribution relationships. Suppliers should clarify the proposed territory and responsibilities, then connect their wine’s identity with a realistic market-development plan.
39. Wine Traditions
Wine Traditions seeks independent growers whose wines express their vineyards and offer accessible value. It operates as a national imp
